title: Find Words on a Letter Grid
statement:
You get a grid board of lowercase letters and a list words of distinct words. A word is on the grid if you can spell it by starting at some cell and stepping each time to a cell that shares a side with the current one (up, down, left or right, never diagonally). Within one word, a cell can be used at most once.

Return every word from words that is on the grid. List each found word once, even if it can be traced in several ways. Any order is accepted.

examples.why: "tea" would need a diagonal step from e to a, and "rest" breaks between s and t. "ace" fails because c touches only a and o.
a and b are neighbours, but "aba" would use the a cell twice. "abdca" fails for the same reason after a full loop.
"oo" can be traced in many places but appears once in the answer. "ooooo" needs five cells and the grid has four.

hints: Searching the grid once per word repeats a lot of work: "cat", "cart" and "care" all start by finding "ca". How could words share that work?
Put all the words into a trie. Then one depth-first search from each cell can follow the trie and check every word with the same prefix at the same time.

Store the full word in the trie node where it ends. When the search reaches such a node, record the word and clear it so it is not reported twice. Remove trie nodes that have nothing left below them, so later searches stop early.

explain.intuition:
Finding a single word on a grid is a backtracking search: from a cell, step into a neighbour with the next letter, mark the cell as used, and undo the mark when you back out. Doing this separately for 30 000 words repeats the same walks again and again, because many words share their first letters.

Turn it around. Put every word into a trie, then run one search from each cell that walks the grid and the trie together. A step into a neighbour is only taken if the trie has a child for that letter, so the search dies as soon as the letters spelled so far are not the start of any word. Each trie node that ends a word holds that word, so reaching it means the word is found. Then two pieces of pruning keep it fast: clear a word once it is found, and delete trie nodes that become empty, so the grid never walks into a dead branch again.
steps: Build a trie of all words. Store the complete word in the node where it ends.
For each cell whose letter is a child of the root, start dfs(r, c, parentNode).
In dfs: move to the child for board[r][c]. If it holds a word, add the word to the answer and clear it.
Mark the cell used (for example set it to #), recurse into each in-bounds neighbour whose letter is a child of the current node, then restore the letter.
After the recursion, if the current node has no children and no word left, delete it from its parent. Return the collected words.
pitfalls: Stopping the search when a word is found. A longer word can continue from the same node: on the grid of example 1, finding "ca" must not stop the search before "cat".
Forgetting to clear a found word. The same word can be traced along several paths and would be added twice, as "oo" in example 3.
Forgetting to restore the cell after backtracking. Later searches then see a # and miss words that use that cell.

complexity.time: O(R · C · 4 · 3^(L−1)) in the worst case, L = longest word; pruning makes it far smaller in practice
complexity.space: O(total letters in words) for the trie

solutions.title: Backtracking search per word
solutions.idea: For each word, try every starting cell and backtrack through neighbours with the next letter. Correct, but repeats shared prefixes for every word.

solutions.title: Trie of words + one search from each cell
solutions.idea: Walk the grid and the trie together. A step is taken only if the trie continues with that letter. Found words are cleared and empty trie nodes deleted.

followups: Diagonal steps are now allowed too. What changes in the code and in the worst-case bound?
The grid stays the same and many different word lists arrive over time. What could you precompute once?
